newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN envoy wants council endorsement for Congo force.
newsitem.headline: UN envoy wants council endorsement for Congo force.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said on Wednesday he intends to ask the Security Council to endorse an African peacekeeping force for the Congo and for the group's wealthier members to pay for it.

Sahnoun, who along with Gabonese President Omar Bongo has been negotiating with the warring parties in the Congolese capital of Brazzaville, said the main conflict concerned presidential elections and who would run them.

"Since neither side trusts the other, both want a peacekeeping force which could supervise a ceasefire and secure the airport to make sure weapons do not flow into the country," he told Reuters. He meets council members Thursday.

A monthlong civil war, which has killed hundreds in Brazzaville, began when President Pascal Lissouba tried to arrest his rival and immediate predecessor, Denis Sassou Nguesso, and disarm his private army.

A mid-June ceasefire was negotiated by the mediators hours after France pulled out the last of its soldiers from Brazzaville. They had helped evacuate nearly 6,000 French and other foreign nationals. But fighting has resumed.

Diplomats said U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan had spoken to them about setting up a special trust fund to pay for a voluntary force and that perhaps a small U.N.-organised peacekeeping force could follow. In addition, Lissouba has offered $1 million to help pay for the peacekeepers.

Sahnoun, who also represents the Organisation of African Unity, said any force had to be endorsed by the Security Council to have legitimacy. A U.N -organised force, he said, would take too long to be authorised and set up, although it had the advantage of being paid for by all members.

But a multi-national force made up mainly of African countries would need outside, voluntary financing. "Without the logistical and financial support necessary to send the force, the process of peace will collapse and have repercussions in the Central African region," Sahnoun said.

Noting that both the United States and several European countries had spoken often of an African peacekeeping force, Sahnoun said the crisis in the Congo "offered a good opportunity for the developed countries, especially those on the Security Council, to go from words to deeds."
France is currently reviewing its Africa policy and does not want to lead a peacekeeping force, diplomats said, although Paris might help with transport or logistics.
Annan on June 21 was authorised by the Security Council to consult with potential troop-contributing countries about sending either a multinational or a U.N. force.

African countries Botswana, Senegal and Togo as well as Bangladesh in Asia have indicated willingness to send troops, U.N. sources said. Annan said the initial size of the force should be no fewer than 1,600 to 1,800, plus support units totalling 400 to 800 as well U.N. military observers.
